Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single Spring MVC application that renders a server-side gallery and handles photo operations. Uploaded image data and metadata are persisted together in Oracle.

Application Architecture

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the production/default database; each Photo record stores metadata and image bytes as a BLOB. H2 is used only by the test profile. No cache, message broker, or external API integration was identified.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A single deployable Spring Boot application owns the presentation, business, and persistence layers.
  • Photo payloads are stored in the relational database rather than on the application filesystem.
  • Reads are public, while upload and delete operations use stateless HTTP Basic authentication.

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application exposes five HTTP routes: three page-oriented GET routes and two write operations. All interactions are synchronous and remain within one application process.

DTOs & Contracts

Photo is the service-level JPA entity used in page models and as the source for photo-file responses. UploadResult is an internal service result; the upload endpoint assembles a response from maps rather than a dedicated request/response DTO. No gateway aggregation DTO, OpenAPI/Swagger specification, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was found. JSON serialization is provided by the Spring Boot JSON/Jackson stack.

Communication Patterns

The browser communicates with the application over synchronous HTTP. Controllers call PhotoService directly; the service calls PhotoRepository, which accesses Oracle through JPA/native SQL. No asynchronous broker, service discovery, application gateway, retry policy, circuit breaker, or inter-service REST client was found. Docker Compose waits for the Oracle health check before starting the application. Stateless HTTP Basic authentication is configured for upload and delete; gallery and read routes are public. TLS termination is not configured in the application files examined.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets a user browse a gallery, upload image files, view individual photos, navigate adjacent uploads, and delete photos. Photos and their metadata are managed as one business concept.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
Photophoto-album / Photo LibraryAn uploaded image plus its display metadata and contentNo other persistent entities; each photo is independently addressable

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
photo-albumPhoto LibraryPhotoOracle database

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload photos

  1. An authenticated user submits one or more multipart files to /upload.
  2. HomeController rejects an empty list, then invokes PhotoService.uploadPhoto for each supplied part.
  3. The service checks the submitted MIME type against its allowlist and checks non-empty content and per-file size. It reads image dimensions when an ImageIO reader recognizes the bytes and rejects images above the configured pixel ceiling.
  4. The service generates an identifier/name, stores the original bytes and metadata on Photo, and saves through PhotoRepository.
  5. The endpoint returns per-file successes and failures. A failed file does not prevent subsequent files in the list from being attempted.

Workflow 2: Browse and view a photo

  1. A visitor opens the gallery; the controller retrieves photos newest-first and renders the page.
  2. Selecting a photo loads its details and asks the service for older/newer items for navigation.
  3. The page requests the photo resource by identifier; the controller returns the database BLOB using the stored MIME type.

Workflow 3: Delete a photo

  1. An authenticated user submits a delete action for a photo identifier.
  2. The service looks up the entity; if absent it reports no deletion.
  3. If present, the service deletes it transactionally and the controller redirects to the gallery with a success or error message.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service composition is implemented. The browser communicates with one application service, which reads and writes Oracle through the repository. Oracle health is a deployment prerequisite in Docker Compose; there is no application-level fallback store.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Gallery user" participant Web as "Photo Album" participant Service as "PhotoService" participant Repo as "PhotoRepository" participant DB as "Oracle database" User->>Web: Submit authenticated image upload Web->>Web: Reject empty file list loop Each uploaded file Web->>Service: Validate and store candidate photo Service->>Service: Check MIME type, size, and image dimensions alt File passes checks Service->>Repo: Save photo and bytes Repo->>DB: Insert photo record DB-->>Repo: Saved photo Repo-->>Service: Photo identifier Service-->>Web: Upload succeeded else File rejected or save fails Service-->>Web: Per-file failure result end end Web-->>User: JSON results for uploaded and failed files

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Accepted MIME values are JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP; validation currently relies on the multipart request's declared content type.
  • A photo must be non-empty and not exceed the configured 10 MiB per-file limit; multipart request size is configured to 50 MiB.
  • Image dimensions are checked from headers when ImageIO identifies a reader; photos over 40 million pixels are rejected.
  • The configuration specifies a maximum of 10 files per upload, but the inspected controller does not enforce that limit.
  • Uploads report results per file; a failed item does not halt processing of later items.
  • Upload and delete require HTTP Basic authentication; reading the gallery and photos is public.
  • Photo service operations use transactional boundaries; no multi-service transaction, compensation, audit subsystem, or explicit state machine was identified.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 and its Spring Framework 5.3/Spring Security 5.7 dependency family are older than current supported release lines. Java 8 compatibility constrains upgrades, and Oracle-specific native queries and the JDBC driver should be included in any runtime/framework modernization review.

Notable Observations

  • Most Spring, Hibernate, Jackson, and test-library versions are inherited from the Spring Boot parent BOM.
  • The Oracle JDBC driver has runtime scope; H2 is test-scoped.
  • Native repository queries include Oracle-specific functions and pagination constructs.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, backed by Oracle in normal and Docker execution and H2 in tests. Hibernate manages the entity model and the repository combines inherited CRUD operations with Oracle-specific native queries.

Caching Strategy

No application cache, cache provider, cache annotations, or Hibernate second-level cache configuration was identified.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The application is a single service with one Oracle database; there are no separate service-owned stores or cross-service database access patterns. Reads and writes go through PhotoService and PhotoRepository; the service is the source of truth for photo metadata and bytes. There is no CQRS or cross-service aggregation.
